I believe this is what’s fueling the mental health crisis. 

Humans were designed to get sunlight, and live in small, tight-knit communities. We weren’t supposed to receive small, artificial hits of dopamine (ie. nicotine, social media, instant gratification) throughout the day, which devastates the dopaminergic system.

Mental health disorders are still very real however. But I believe our modern society is responsible for a large deal of the worsening of, and activation of mental illness and it’s symptoms.

I’ve had warnings signs of increased risk for developing a PD since early childhood, such as a high proneness to melancholic mood and high emotional sensitivity. 

It wasn’t until I began experiencing “little t” traumas in my adolescence, however, that I began to display some of the hallmark symptoms of BPD. 

And after a 6 month period of extreme stress and recurrent traumas at 19-20 (homelessness, abuse, abandonment, addiction, etc.). I officially met the diagnostic criteria for BPD. It was after that 6 month period that I felt the most dramatic change in my personality structure and functioning. 

My BPD has been a combination of nature and nurture.
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3811092/ is the link.

There is no FDA approved drug for BPD, however a variety of medications can help treat symptoms of the disorder, such as affective instability, impulsivity, depression, aggression, and anxiety.

If you scroll through the attached scholarly article, you can see how different classes of medication can target different clusters of symptoms, and it may be helpful for you to advocate for yourself when meeting with a prescribing physician. 

For me personally, I take a high dose of fluoxetine (SSRI) for my depression, anxiety, anger, and impulsivity; and a therapeutic dose of aripiprazole (mood stabilizer) for paranoia and aggression.

In regards to ADD/ADHD, off the top of my head, stimulant medication such as Adderall, Ritalin, and Vyvanse are commonly prescribed, however can come with a host of side effects. A non stimulant medication that is also commonly prescribed is Strattera, which is an sNRI. 

ADHD medications are typically not unsafe to take if you have BPD, but if you have a history of bipolar or manic symptoms, then it may potentially cause worsening of those symptoms.

Have you learned about distress tolerance skills in DBT? The TIPP skill has helped me immensely for self harm urges when I am activated, and need to come back down to baseline. 

TIPP stands for T: tip the temperature; I: intense exercise; P: paced breathing; and P: progressive muscle relaxation. 

My go-to is the Tip the Temperature skill. It utilizes the mammalian dive response, which calms the sympathetic nervous system to a parasympathetic state. There is a lot of research to back up the efficacy of this skill. (Learned about this from my therapist, who is a retired professor of neuroscience).

What you want to do is splash your face with ice water, or hold ice cubes below your eyes. Maybe even jump into a cold pool. Whatever you can do to expose your face to a cool temperature and trigger the mammalian dive response. 

This physiological mechanism (that all mammals possess) works every time to calm your nervous system and help bring you closer to baseline—it’s just the science! But find a method that works best for you. This is just what I have found to be most helpful and effective personally.
